statute_title: Driving Under the Influence / Driving While Impaired
elements: Defendant drove or attempted to drive a vehicle
While under the influence of alcohol (DUI) or while impaired by alcohol (DWI)
Or with a BAC of .08 or higher (DUI) or .07+ (DWI)
notes: Maryland distinguishes between DUI (.08+ BAC) and DWI (.07+ BAC or impaired). Noah's Law (2016) requires ignition interlock for all DUI/DWI convictions. 12 points assessed.

elements: Defendant drove or attempted to drive a vehicle
While under the influence of alcohol or with BAC .08+
No prior DUI convictions
notes: Noah's Law requires ignition interlock device for all first-offense DUI convictions. License suspension up to 6 months.

elements: Defendant drove or attempted to drive a vehicle
While under the influence of alcohol or with BAC .08+
One or more prior DUI/DWI convictions
notes: Second offense: mandatory 5 days jail. Third+: mandatory 10 days. Extended ignition interlock period. License revocation up to 1 year.

elements: Defendant drove or attempted to drive a vehicle
While so far impaired by a drug, combination of drugs, or combination of drugs and alcohol
That the defendant could not drive safely
enhancements: Combined influence of drugs and alcohol
notes: No per se drug limit. Drug Recognition Expert (DRE) evaluation and toxicology used. Same penalties as alcohol DUI.

elements: Defendant drove a vehicle in willful or wanton disregard for the safety of persons or property
notes: 6 points on license. Negligent driving (§ 21-901.1(b)) is a lesser offense. Common plea-down from DUI.

statute_title: Failure to Remain at Scene — Bodily Injury or Death
elements: Defendant was the driver of a vehicle involved in an accident
Accident resulted in bodily injury or death
Defendant failed to stop and remain at the scene
Defendant failed to provide identification and render aid
notes: Hit-and-run resulting in death is a felony. Property damage only (§ 20-103) carries up to 60 days and $500.

elements: Defendant caused the death of another person
As a result of driving a motor vehicle in a grossly negligent manner
enhancements: Under the influence of alcohol or drugs at time of incident
notes: Separate from criminal negligent manslaughter by vehicle (§ 2-501.1) which carries up to 3 years.

elements: Defendant caused the death of another person
As a result of driving a motor vehicle in a criminally negligent manner
notes: Lesser offense than manslaughter by vehicle (§ 2-501). Criminal negligence is a lower standard than gross negligence.

statute_title: Driving While License Suspended or Revoked
elements: Defendant drove a motor vehicle on a highway or public property
Defendant's license was suspended or revoked
Defendant had knowledge or notice of the suspension or revocation
notes: Driving on suspended carries additional license suspension. May result in vehicle impoundment.

statute_title: Fleeing or Attempting to Elude Police
offense_class: Misdemeanor (general); Felony (if causing life-threatening injury or death)
elements: A police officer signaled the defendant to stop
Signal was by visual or audible means
Defendant willfully failed to stop
Defendant attempted to flee or elude the officer
notes: Officer must be in uniform or in a marked vehicle. Felony enhancement if serious injury or death results.

elements: Defendant possessed a controlled dangerous substance
Substance is listed in Maryland CDS schedules
Possession was without a valid prescription or lawful authority
notes: Maryland decriminalized marijuana under 10g (civil citation). 10g-2.5oz is a misdemeanor. Over 2.5oz may trigger intent to distribute charges.

offense_class: Civil Citation (under 10g); Misdemeanor (10g-2.5oz); Felony (2.5oz+ with intent)
elements: Defendant possessed cannabis
Amount exceeded legal personal use limits for adults 21+
enhancements: Possession over 2.5 oz without valid registration
notes: Maryland legalized recreational cannabis for adults 21+ in July 2023 (up to 1.5 oz usable, 12g concentrate). Amounts over 2.5 oz without registration remain criminal. Under 21 possession remains a civil violation.

elements: Defendant possessed cocaine
Cocaine is a Schedule II controlled dangerous substance in Maryland
Possession was without lawful authority
notes: Simple possession is a misdemeanor. Larger quantities may support distribution charges.

elements: Defendant possessed methamphetamine
Methamphetamine is a Schedule II controlled dangerous substance
Possession was without lawful authority
notes: Simple possession carries up to 4 years. Manufacturing meth is charged separately under § 5-603.

elements: Defendant brought a controlled dangerous substance into Maryland
Or manufactured, distributed, or possessed with intent to distribute
Quantity met or exceeded trafficking thresholds
notes: Drug trafficking carries a mandatory 5-year minimum that cannot be suspended. Thresholds vary by substance: 448g cocaine, 28g heroin, 5g fentanyl.

elements: Defendant distributed, dispensed, or possessed with intent to distribute a CDS
Substance is listed in Maryland CDS schedules
notes: Second offense for Schedule I/II narcotics: up to 20 years. Third offense: mandatory minimum 25 years.

elements: Defendant manufactured, created, or produced a controlled dangerous substance
enhancements: Manufacturing near a school or child care facility
notes: Manufacturing methamphetamine carries additional environmental and child endangerment charges. Cleanup costs may be assessed.

elements: Defendant used or possessed with intent to use drug paraphernalia
To plant, propagate, cultivate, grow, harvest, manufacture, compound, convert, produce, process, prepare, test, analyze, pack, repack, store, contain, or conceal a CDS
enhancements: Sale or delivery to a minor
notes: Maryland decriminalized paraphernalia associated with marijuana. Paraphernalia for other drugs remains criminal.

statute_title: Possession with Intent to Distribute CDS
elements: Defendant possessed a controlled dangerous substance
With intent to distribute
notes: Intent inferred from quantity, packaging, scales, cash, communications. Same penalties as actual distribution.

elements: Defendant willfully, deliberately, and with premeditation killed another person
Or killed another person during the commission of a felony (felony murder)
mandatory_minimum: Life without parole (if defendant was 18+, certain circumstances)
enhancements: Murder of a law enforcement officer
Murder during commission of certain felonies
notes: Maryland abolished the death penalty in 2013. First-degree murder includes premeditated killing, felony murder, and murder by poison or lying in wait.

elements: Defendant killed another person
With intent to kill or with implied malice
But without premeditation or deliberation
notes: Includes intentional killings without premeditation and depraved-heart murder (extreme recklessness showing disregard for human life).

elements: Defendant intentionally killed another person
The killing occurred in the heat of passion
Upon adequate provocation
notes: Heat of passion reduces what would otherwise be murder to manslaughter. Must be provocation that would cause a reasonable person to lose self-control.

elements: Defendant caused the death of another person
Through grossly negligent or reckless conduct
Without intent to kill
notes: Common law offense codified in Maryland. Includes deaths resulting from criminal negligence and unlawful acts not amounting to felonies.

elements: Defendant committed an assault
Defendant intended to cause serious physical injury
Or used a firearm to commit the assault
mandatory_minimum: 10 years (if firearm used, mandatory minimum under § 4-305)
enhancements: Use of a firearm (mandatory minimum 10 years for subsequent)
Victim was a law enforcement officer
notes: First-degree assault is the most serious assault charge in Maryland. Use of a firearm triggers mandatory minimum under separate statute.

elements: Defendant committed an assault, battery, or threatened assault against another person
enhancements: Victim is a law enforcement officer (§ 3-203(c), up to 10 years)
notes: Maryland merged assault and battery into a single offense. Second-degree assault is the general misdemeanor assault.

elements: Defendant committed an assault
Defendant used a firearm or other dangerous weapon
enhancements: Victim was a law enforcement officer
notes: Assault with a firearm constitutes first-degree assault automatically. Other weapons must be shown to be dangerous in the manner used.

elements: Defendant committed or attempted to commit theft
Defendant used force or threat of force to obtain property
Or placed the victim in fear of force
enhancements: Use of a dangerous weapon (armed robbery under § 3-403)
notes: Robbery in Maryland is a common law felony. No weapon is required — force or fear is sufficient.

elements: Defendant committed or attempted to commit theft
Defendant used a dangerous weapon during the robbery
Or displayed what appeared to be a dangerous weapon
notes: Armed robbery carries up to 20 years — 5 more than unarmed robbery. Display of a replica weapon is sufficient.

elements: Defendant forcibly seized, confined, carried, or transported another person
Without consent and without lawful authority
notes: Child kidnapping (§ 3-503) carries up to 25 years. False imprisonment (§ 3-405) is a lesser included offense.

elements: Defendant willfully and maliciously set fire to or burned a structure
Structure was a dwelling or occupied structure
notes: First-degree arson involves occupied structures. Second-degree (§ 6-103) involves unoccupied structures, up to 20 years.

elements: Defendant took a substantial step toward intentionally killing another person
With specific intent to kill
With willfulness, deliberation, and premeditation
enhancements: Victim was a law enforcement officer
notes: Attempted first-degree murder carries the same maximum as completed first-degree murder. Attempted second-degree murder carries up to 30 years.

elements: Defendant willfully or knowingly obtained control over property of another
By deception, willful concealment, or unauthorized taking
With intent to deprive the owner
notes: Maryland consolidated theft offenses under a single statute. Value thresholds determine misdemeanor vs. felony classification.

elements: Defendant willfully or knowingly obtained control over property of another
Value of property was $1,500 or more
With intent to deprive the owner
notes: Felony theft threshold is $1,500 in Maryland.

elements: Defendant willfully or knowingly obtained control over property of another
Value of property was under $1,500
With intent to deprive the owner
notes: Under $100 is a petty misdemeanor. $100–$1,500 is a regular misdemeanor.

offense_class: Same as general theft by value
penalty_max: Same as general theft by value
fine_max: Same as general theft by value
elements: Defendant willfully concealed or took possession of retail merchandise
Without paying full consideration
With intent to deprive the merchant
notes: Shoplifting is charged under the general theft statute. Merchants may also pursue civil penalties.

elements: Defendant broke into and entered a storehouse or other structure
With intent to commit theft or a crime of violence
enhancements: Person was present in the structure
notes: Second-degree burglary covers non-dwelling structures. First-degree burglary (§ 6-201) involves dwellings.

elements: Defendant broke into and entered a dwelling
With intent to commit a crime of violence
notes: First-degree burglary requires a dwelling and intent to commit a crime of violence. If intent is only theft, it may be charged as third-degree.

statute_title: Unauthorized Use of a Motor Vehicle
elements: Defendant knowingly and willfully took or used a motor vehicle
Without the consent of the owner
notes: Separate from general theft. May also be charged as theft if intent to permanently deprive is proven.

offense_class: Same as general theft by value
penalty_max: Same as general theft by value
fine_max: Same as general theft by value
elements: Defendant received, retained, or disposed of property of another
Knowing or having reason to believe the property was stolen
notes: Charged under the general theft statute. Same value thresholds and penalties as other theft offenses.

elements: Defendant willfully and maliciously destroyed, damaged, or defaced property of another
notes: Includes graffiti and property destruction. Restitution typically ordered.

elements: Defendant entered or crossed over posted property of another
After being notified not to enter by posted signs or fencing
notes: Wanton trespass on private property (§ 6-403) carries similar penalties. Trespass on a railroad carries specific penalties.

elements: Defendant willfully and maliciously damaged or destroyed property of another
notes: Maryland uses 'malicious destruction of property' as the statutory term. Covers vandalism, graffiti, and other property damage.

elements: Defendant committed an assault against a person in a domestic relationship
Domestic relationship includes spouse, former spouse, cohabitant, parent of common child, or relative
notes: Maryland charges DV under general assault statutes with domestic relationship as a factor. Protective orders available under Family Law § 4-501.

elements: Defendant committed a battery against a person in a domestic relationship
Battery involves unwanted physical contact
notes: Maryland merged assault and battery. No separate battery statute. DV cases handled under second-degree assault.

offense_class: Misdemeanor (first degree); Felony (if cause of death)
elements: Defendant was a parent, guardian, or custodian of a minor
Defendant failed to provide proper care and attention
Under circumstances creating a substantial risk of harm to the child
notes: Separate from child abuse (§ 3-601). Neglect focuses on failure to provide care rather than affirmative harmful conduct.

elements: Defendant caused severe physical injury to a child under 18
Through an intentional or knowing act
notes: First-degree requires severe physical injury. Second-degree (§ 3-601(b)) involves abuse without severe injury, up to 15 years.

elements: A valid protective order was in effect
Defendant had notice of the order
Defendant violated a provision of the order
notes: Mandatory arrest for violations. Federal firearms prohibition applies while protective order is in effect.

elements: Defendant engaged in a persistent pattern of conduct
Directed at a specific person
That would cause a reasonable person to fear death, bodily injury, or assault
Or the conduct placed the victim in reasonable fear
notes: Includes cyberstalking. Harassment (§ 3-803) is a related lesser offense.

elements: Defendant followed or engaged in a course of conduct directed at a specific person
With intent to harass, alarm, or annoy
After being warned to stop
notes: Includes electronic and telephone harassment. Lesser offense than stalking.

statute_title: Abuse or Neglect of a Vulnerable Adult
elements: Defendant caused physical injury, sexual abuse, or severe emotional abuse to a vulnerable adult
Defendant was a household member, caretaker, or person with authority
notes: Vulnerable adult includes persons 68+ and disabled adults. Financial exploitation is a separate offense under § 8-801.

statute_title: Wearing, Carrying, or Transporting a Handgun
elements: Defendant wore, carried, or transported a handgun
On or about the person
Without a valid permit
mandatory_minimum: 30 days (second offense, no suspension); 3 years (third+, no suspension)
notes: Post-Bruen (2022), Maryland's permit process changed significantly. Carry restrictions near certain sensitive locations remain. Second and third offenses carry mandatory minimums.

statute_title: Possession of Regulated Firearm by Prohibited Person
elements: Defendant possessed a regulated firearm
Defendant had a prior felony conviction or was otherwise a prohibited person
mandatory_minimum: 5 years (cannot be suspended or paroled before serving)
enhancements: Possession during commission of a crime
notes: Mandatory minimum of 5 years that cannot be suspended. One of the most strictly enforced firearms offenses in Maryland.

elements: Defendant carried a handgun on or about the person
Without a valid wear-and-carry permit
notes: Maryland transitioned to shall-issue permits following the Bruen decision. Sensitive location restrictions remain in effect.

statute_title: Discharge of Firearm from Motor Vehicle
elements: Defendant discharged a firearm from a motor vehicle
In a manner that created a risk of death or injury to another
notes: Mandatory 5-year minimum without suspension. Separate from reckless endangerment.

elements: Defendant knowingly, willfully, and with fraudulent intent used personal identifying information of another
To obtain money, goods, services, or other benefit
notes: Includes Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers, financial account information.

elements: Defendant was entrusted with property in a fiduciary capacity
Defendant fraudulently converted the property to personal use
notes: May also be charged under general theft statutes. Fiduciary misappropriation carries separate penalties.

elements: Defendant falsely made, altered, or counterfeited a document
With intent to defraud
enhancements: Forgery of public documents or currency
notes: Separate statutes for private documents (§ 8-601) and public documents (§ 8-602). Both carry up to 10 years.

elements: Defendant made, possessed, or uttered counterfeit currency or government obligations
notes: Federal counterfeiting charges typically apply. State charges may be concurrent.

elements: Defendant obtained property, services, or credit by issuing a check
Knowing there were insufficient funds in the account
With intent to defraud
notes: Value thresholds align with general theft. Restitution typically ordered.

fine_max: $100,000 or triple the amount of the fraudulent claim
elements: Defendant knowingly presented a false or fraudulent insurance claim
With intent to defraud or deceive an insurer
notes: Maryland Insurance Administration investigates. Separate from general theft by deception.

elements: Defendant used a credit card or credit card number
Knowing it was stolen, counterfeit, or without authorization
To obtain goods, services, or money
notes: Includes possession of stolen credit cards and use of credit card numbers obtained through fraud.

elements: Defendant conducted a financial transaction
Knowing the transaction involved proceeds of criminal activity
With intent to promote criminal activity or conceal the source
notes: Drug-related money laundering under § 5-623. General financial crimes laundering also applies.

offense_class: Same as general theft by value
penalty_max: Same as general theft by value
fine_max: Same as general theft by value
elements: Defendant obtained property or services through deception
Deception includes creating false impressions, preventing acquisition of relevant information, or failing to disclose known defects
With intent to deprive the owner
notes: General fraud charged under the consolidated theft statute. Classification by value.

elements: Defendant engaged in vaginal intercourse with another by force or threat of force
Without consent of the victim
Or the victim was under 13
notes: First-degree rape is the most serious sex offense. Second-degree rape (§ 3-304) carries up to 20 years.

elements: Defendant engaged in vaginal intercourse by force or threat of force
Without consent
Using a weapon, threat of force, suffocation, or strangulation
notes: Maryland defines rape under four degrees. First-degree carries life imprisonment.

elements: Defendant exposed their person or genitals
In a public place or in the sight of another
Under circumstances likely to be observed
notes: May require sex offender registration depending on circumstances.

elements: Defendant offered or agreed to engage in a sexual act
In exchange for compensation
notes: Solicitation involving a minor is a felony carrying up to 10 years. General prostitution also up to 1 year.

elements: Defendant engaged in sexual contact or a sexual act with a minor
Defendant was a household member, family member, or person in a position of authority
notes: Covers sexual abuse by household members and persons in authority. Child pornography offenses under § 11-207.

statute_title: Failure to Register as Sex Offender
elements: Defendant was required to register as a sex offender
Defendant knowingly failed to register or update registration information
notes: Maryland Sex Offender Registry. Registration periods: Tier I (15 years), Tier II (25 years), Tier III (lifetime).

elements: Defendant engaged in vaginal intercourse with a person under 14
Defendant was at least 4 years older than the victim
notes: Age of consent in Maryland is 16. Close-in-age exception: if victim is 14-15 and defendant is less than 4 years older.

statute_title: Disturbing the Public Peace — Disorderly Conduct
elements: Defendant willfully acted in a disorderly manner
That disturbed the public peace
notes: Low-level public order offense. Often charged alongside other offenses.

elements: A law enforcement officer attempted to make a lawful arrest or detention
Defendant intentionally resisted, interfered with, or obstructed the officer
notes: Includes both physical resistance and flight. Assault on a law enforcement officer is a separate, more serious charge.

elements: Defendant obstructed, hindered, or prevented a law enforcement officer
In the performance of official duties
Defendant acted with knowledge that the person was a law enforcement officer
notes: Broader than resisting arrest. Covers any interference with police duties.

penalty_max: Varies by court; typically up to 30 days or until compliance
elements: A valid court order was in effect
Defendant had knowledge of the order
Defendant willfully disobeyed the order
notes: Constructive contempt (out of court) and direct contempt (in court) have different procedures. Civil contempt is coercive.

elements: Defendant appeared in a public place while intoxicated
Defendant's conduct was disorderly or created a public nuisance
notes: Maryland does not have a standalone public intoxication statute. Charged under disorderly conduct.

elements: Defendant was released on bail or personal recognizance
Defendant was required to appear in court
Defendant willfully failed to appear
notes: Bench warrant issued upon failure to appear. May also result in bail forfeiture.

statute_title: False Statement to Law Enforcement Officer
elements: Defendant made a false statement to a law enforcement officer
Regarding the commission of a crime
Knowing the statement was false
notes: Separate from perjury (sworn testimony). Applies to statements made during investigations.

offense_class: Misdemeanor (general threats under § 3-707); Felony (mass violence threats)
penalty_max: 10 years (mass violence); 3 years (general threats to public officials under § 3-708)
elements: Defendant threatened to commit an act of mass violence
At a place of public use, government facility, or place of worship
notes: Threat of mass violence statute enacted 2019. General threatening is charged as second-degree assault or harassment.

elements: Defendant made a false statement under oath
In a judicial or official proceeding
Knowing the statement was false
Statement was material to the proceeding
notes: Includes testimony, depositions, and sworn affidavits.

elements: Defendant offered, gave, or promised a benefit to a public employee
With intent to influence the employee's official action
notes: Covers both offering and receiving bribes. Bribery of a juror is a separate offense under § 9-202.

elements: Defendant was confined in a place of confinement
Defendant departed without authorization or failed to return
notes: First-degree escape is from confinement. Second-degree (§ 9-405) is from custody (arrest, transport). Third-degree is leaving temporary release.

elements: Defendant intentionally mutilated, tortured, or cruelly killed an animal
Or caused or procured the same
notes: Aggravated cruelty is a felony. General cruelty, overworking, and neglect are misdemeanors.

penalty_max: Up to the maximum of the original sentence
elements: Defendant was on probation for a criminal conviction
Defendant violated a condition of probation
enhancements: New criminal offense while on probation
notes: Court may revoke probation and impose any sentence available at the time of original conviction. Graduated sanctions may be used.

elements: Defendant was on parole from a correctional institution
Defendant violated a condition of parole
notes: Maryland Parole Commission conducts revocation hearings. Violator may serve remainder of original sentence.

statute_title: Accessory Before the Fact / Aiding and Abetting
elements: Defendant aided, abetted, advised, or encouraged another person
In the commission of a crime
notes: An accessory before the fact is liable to the same extent as the principal. Maryland common law and statutory provisions apply.

offense_class: Same as the target offense (common law)
elements: Defendant intended to commit a specific crime
Defendant took a substantial step toward commission of the crime
Beyond mere preparation
notes: Maryland follows common law attempt doctrine. Attempt carries the same penalty as the completed offense for most crimes.

offense_class: Same as the target offense (common law)
elements: Defendant agreed with one or more persons to commit a crime
An overt act was performed in furtherance of the conspiracy
notes: Maryland follows common law conspiracy principles. Conspiracy carries the same penalty as the completed offense.

elements: Defendant knowingly took or caused another person to be taken to any place
For the purpose of prostitution, sexual exploitation, or forced labor
Through force, fraud, or coercion
notes: Maryland enacted comprehensive anti-trafficking laws. Victims may seek civil remedies. Safe harbor provisions for minor victims.

elements: Defendant intentionally confined or restrained another person
Without consent and without lawful authority
notes: Common law offense. Lesser included offense of kidnapping. No specific statutory maximum — court discretion.

elements: Defendant possessed an opioid drug (heroin, fentanyl, or similar)
Opioid is a Schedule I or II controlled dangerous substance
Possession was without lawful authority
notes: Maryland focuses enforcement on distribution rather than simple possession. Diversion programs available for first-time offenders.

elements: Defendant obtained unauthorized possession of a motor vehicle from another
By force, violence, or intimidation
Or by threat of force, violence, or intimidation
notes: Armed carjacking carries the same 30-year maximum. Carjacking is one of the most aggressively prosecuted offenses in Maryland.
